title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
description: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.As part of Wedn
body: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats."AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said."I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI."One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops."That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said."By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

schema.headline: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

title: Met investigates reports of letter detailing claims about Meghan's father
description: Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years
body: Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years ago.According to the Sun, the letter was sent to a Met Police unit tasked with dealing with individuals posing a threat to Royals and politicians - the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre.A Met spokesperson said: "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018."We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines in 2025 after a series of strokes.He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025.In her statement on Friday, Meghan said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father in 2018, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun that he had allegedly found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police.The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Investigators there are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results.The US Federal Bureau of Investigations said it was "aware of the allegations", adding it would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".The FBI's statement continued: "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage.The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018.At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding.It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father shortly after she married the Duke of Sussex Prince Harry.Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation.Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said.

schema.headline: Met investigates reports of letter detailing claims about Meghan's father

title: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?
description: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fun
body: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries? One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate. The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries. And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes. If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows. However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK? Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund. But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.But there are two issues to consider. Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes). Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing. As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap. The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men. But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere. But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action. The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

schema.headline: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Meghan warned over father' and 'Don't risk Truss-style budget'
description: The Duchess of Sussex appears on many of the front pages. The Daily Mail, external leads with the Met searching for the letter it received containing
body: The Duchess of Sussex appears on many of the front pages. The Daily Mail, external leads with the Met searching for the letter it received containing allegations about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle. The Daily Telegraph, external says it understands she was advised against speaking about it publicly in 2018, in case it jeopardised any subsequent investigation. The Sun, external makes further allegations about Thomas Markle and says Meghan's statement on Friday was "brave and impactful". Thomas Markle denies possessing child sex images.The Financial Times, external says £20bn of extra funding will be announced for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank in next week's Budget. The intention is for the money to create 100,000 jobs in sectors like AI, defence, and green energy by 2035. The additional borrowing to support the lending is expected to begin in 2028.Andy Haldane, the former chief economist at the Bank of England has told the Times, external that he fears a "mañana budget" that defers difficult decisions, even though he says the country is "close to being taxed out and maxed out, in terms of borrowing". Haldane, who acted as an informal advisor to Andy Burnham during his time as Greater Manchester mayor, called the economy the prime minister's "blind spot".The cabinet is split on the issue of whether or not the UK should seek to rejoin the EU, the i Weekend, external says. A narrow majority of ministers favours rejoining, but the paper says there is no consensus on whether or not a referendum would be held, or whether or not the ambition risks re-opening the wounds of Brexit.An archaeologist for Historic England says he's resolved the long-running debate about which pub is the oldest in the country. Around two dozen establishments have claimed the status for themselves, but now the Guardian, external and the Daily Mail , externalsay Dr James Wright has settled the matter. Having checked building purposes, tree-ring dating on wooden beams, and researching existing surviving fabrics, the title goes to te George Inn, in Norton St Philip, in Somerset. Dr Wright says it has been in continuous service for more than 600 years.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Meghan warned over father' and 'Don't risk Truss-style budget'

title: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast
description: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nat
body: To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes."There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us."The wildlife will approach you sometimes."Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular."In theory, they should have migrated."Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks. Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.

schema.headline: Moment giant fin whale caught feeding off Pembrokeshire coast

title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
description: Image source, ReutersBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesFew places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US stat
body: Image source, ReutersBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesFew places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to many rich and famous.Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades."I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill."If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.Image source, Getty ImagesWhile the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth taxThe California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax."I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he said, adding that the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy."I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule". "They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy."This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

schema.headline: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?

title: Celebrity Traitors, episode eight: Series left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
description: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest re
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife as to whodunnit and why?The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before."I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried."Oh bottoms!""I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally."Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson"."Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added.Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six, said she was now praying that the heat on her would now cool down.While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through".Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however."This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast."We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second."Wink, wink.Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed."But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, "OG Traits", still flying it up."Joanne had earlier joked that Maya would not be killed or banished as "she's too hot. The hot ones always survive."After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent."He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work."With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool, Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something."How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh."It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming.Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners".On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows."This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying."The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot.Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold."I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared.But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants.Things got a bit awkward when poor Sharon "got so mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll.In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny."I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'."With the others en route back to the castle, Winkleman quipped to the traitors: "This is like an outdoor turret."The special power was revealed to be a double dagger enabling "the trustworthy trio", as James A is now calling them, to award two banishment votes to whoever they wanted to hold it.King Kenny became King Arthur being crowned keeper of the special blade."I think it's in the right hands," declared James B back at the castle, now colder than ever in terms of catching a traitor."I feel like whoever it is, they are five sreps ahead of us," noted a befuddled Leigh-Anne. "We don't have a clue!"Romesh then had to remind Joanne that her policy of not voting off Michael because he's "great company" is not really how the game should work.With the double dagger in play and time running out for the faithful, Michael declared that he had to catch a traitor tonight.Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and FridayThe latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedAs discussions began, double trouble Kenny warned: "Be nice to me everyone!""You're a powerful man," noted Joanne.Bash, who had flown under the radar until this point, drew some heat along with Leigh-Anne and Sharon at another roundtable led my Don Michael."If you're a faithful, why are you still here?" Bash asked the Welshman, who noted he had a shield last time out.Romesh agreed: "I definitely would have killed you by now if I was a traitor. And I mean that as a massive compliment, because I think, for the morale of the group, you not being here would decimate us."In an attempt to deflect attention away from himself, Michael stressed how Sharon had been acting like a "totally different person" of late.Kenny bought it, sticking his double dagger into the Barbie actress. And James B voted the same way due to her "suspicious" actions earlier on.Scotswoman Sharon received four votes, along with Irish comic Joanne, meaning that - after desperate final pleas from the pair - it went to second round. "Do whatever youse want, it's a game," offered a seemingly defeated Sharon."I wish I didn't take this dagger," said Kenny, ahead of his decisive second thrust of the double blade. "But I'm gonna vote for..."The producers then left things, quite literally, on a knife edge.Ten contestant remain (for now): seven faithfuls (soon to be six) and three traitors, putting the cloaked interlopers in a great position going into the final two episodes. With the hurly-burly done for another week, we will wait with baited breath until Hallowe'en's double header to see how the battle will be lost and won.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors, episode eight: Series left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams

title: France prepares for day of protest a week after nationwide riots
description: France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the country saw some of its worst unrest in decades.Sweepi
body: France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the country saw some of its worst unrest in decades.Sweeping restrictions have been imposed on demonstrations across France but hundreds of thousands of protesters are still expected to gather in Paris and elsewhere for a second round of protests organised by students, trade unions and wider anti-government groups.The interior ministry has said it will deploy 70,000 police officers, ramping up the security presence in French cities, after the government was accused by opposition parties of failing to foresee the scale of the unrest on 17 October."We will not let anything go unchallenged," said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez."We will be uncompromising with the vandals, with the looters, and all those who commit acts of violence," he added, explaining that separate from the planned protests, numerous calls for violence had been seen on social media from the "far left and radical extreme left".Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.Disillusionment is high among the French public, who have seen cost-of-living pressures increase and who are faced with increasingly dire warnings that any future government will likely come with deep spending cuts.The protests began with demands from high school students to improve school conditions and fix staff shortages, before violence took hold in places.President Emmanuel Macron met high-school students' representatives on Friday ahead of Saturday's protests, and although they said he had made clear commitments to them, they said students should "continue to mobilise".Macron told them his government would make a series of commitments to improve high school education from Monday, his advisers told French TV.In a sign of how a student-led protest movement expanded to become a wider anti-government outpouring, protesters associated with a revived gilet jaunes (yellow-vest) movement could be out in force across France on Saturday.The protest movement, which has attracted support from both the left and right, led huge disruptive demonstrations during Macron's first term in office.A website associated with the group listed more than 500 planned demonstrations and 200 other actions on Saturday, and demanded that Macron resign. The group said "we refuse to add our voices to the chorus of outrage" over the violence on 17 October and accused police of attacking protesters.France is still reeling from last week's unrest, which saw police vastly outnumbered by protesters and rioters, shops looted and buildings torched - perhaps most emblematically, the ornate 19th-Century town hall in Limoges.French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said while visiting Limoges on Friday that the national government would pay for the building to be reconstructed "exactly as it was" rather than local taxpayers having to foot the bill.Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 232 people had been imprisoned for their role in the 17 October riots and more than 1,100 others had appeared in court. Around 260 of those cases involves "charges of organised gang activity", he added.Darmanin has ordered prosecutors to seek punitive measures against people convicted of looting or attacking police officers, including banning them from taking part in demonstrations, removing their right to vote and barring them from accessing social media.The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape and with France preparing for what could be the most divisive and unpredictable election period in a generation.Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest a candidate from his centrist movement could fail to make it through to a run-off vote in May.That would likely leave French voters to choose between the hard-right National Rally and radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron and his ministers, sensing fertile ground among the French public after a period in which his centrist party has struggled to form functioning governments and pass legislation. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader and presidential candidate of LFI, has criticised what he has framed as heavy-handed policing of demonstrations and accused Macron of "destroying the republican state" by imposing restrictions.He has called on his supporters to join protests on Saturday, as he did the previous week, before condemning the rioting that followed.A two-day National Rally conference in Orléans, around 120km (75 miles) to the south of Paris, could prove to be a flashpoint on Saturday. Left-wing groups are expected to descend on the small city, where thousands of members of the hard-right party are set to gather to hear its leader Marine Le Pen speak.This week, the city's mayor warned the numbers expected in Orléans were "unprecedented" and said thousands of police would be deployed to manage any clashes, adding that public transport would be suspended.Opinion polls suggest Le Pen could have her strongest chance yet of becoming president as she runs for a fourth time, despite a court finding her guilty of embezzling EU funds earlier this year. She has denied committing any offence and is appealing the verdict.

schema.headline: France prepares for day of protest a week after nationwide riots

title: How to heat your home without turning on the heating
description: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep your house warmer for longerImage source, Cora HarrisonImage caption, Cora Harrison says sh
body: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep your house warmer for longerImage source, Cora HarrisonImage caption, Cora Harrison says she saves money by only turning on heating in rooms her family is usingByGrace DeanAs the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all.But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run.Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health.To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective.Eat hearty winter meals to warm you throughWhen it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body.The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference".Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm. Image source, Amber WaringImage caption, Amber Waring turns to warming meals such as pasta bake, fish pie and stew  Place a blanket under the bedsheetWith the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in. So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.Open curtains and let the sun in during the dayKeep doors closed to trap heat in the room you're in. You can place curtains or blankets over your doors for extra insulation.Embrace the daylight. "If it's sunny outside, open the curtains so the sun heats the room, then shut them when the sun sets to keep the heat in," says Rebecca.Image source, Olga Pankova/Getty ImagesImage caption, Sunlight can help keep rooms comfortable for longer before you need to switch the heating on"If you're using a hot appliance, let the heat into the room," says Lianne Macfarlane, 40, from Cheshire. She recommends leaving your oven door open after using it to help warm your kitchen, though this isn't advised if you have small children who could injure themselves.As well as curtains, other soft furnishings like rugs can help keep a room warm, says Seymour.Image source, Elin DavisImage caption, Elin Davis fires up her log burner when it gets coldIf you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you're in can be cheaper than turning on the central heating for your whole house. Elin Davis, 30, from South Wales, says her log burner is more economical than turning her heating on - though she added that "logs can cost quite a bit these days".Insulate your windows with bubble wrapGaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights.When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds.If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows.Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, If you're after cheap insulation, especially if your window panes are single-glazed, then placing bubble wrap on them might helpUse central heating wisely"I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over.But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat.You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls.Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family is using and keeps the heating on at a low level when they're on holiday to avoid mould or pipes bursting. Some radiators have a snowflake symbol on the valve that activates the frost protection setting, meaning that if the room gets very cold, the radiator warms slightly to stop the pipes from bursting.Another way to potentially reduce energy bills is to lower the flow temperature of your combi boiler. If you book a boiler service, an engineer can do this for you.You can also find free warm spaces such as libraries and community centres in your area by looking online or contacting the council. Some spaces also provide free hot drinks.Will energy bills rise further?Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill expected to jump by £276 a year, according to a forecast last month from consultancy Cornwall Insight. The 16% predicted increase would mark the biggest rise for four years.Rising bills are "particularly concerning for people with kids, people with health conditions and the elderly," says Emily Jeremy, project manager at Manchester South Central Foodbank.An estimated 9.4% of households in England lived in fuel poverty in 2025, according to the latest government figures, external.Rodney Winchester, 65, from Thetford, who spoke to BBC News through the charity Christians Against Poverty, says he's "extremely worried" about rising energy prices. Because of health conditions, he says he has to keep the heating on throughout winter but is concerned he won't be able to afford it."It's so scary," Rodney says, adding that he's been cutting back on food spending and keeps getting ill in the cold weather.If you are struggling with prices, the debt charity StepChange recommends checking whether you qualify for any additional support, like the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment. It also advises contacting your energy supplier, which may be able to agree an affordable repayment plan or discuss support schemes.

schema.headline: How to heat your home without turning on the heating

title: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?
description: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?Image caption, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess
body: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?Image caption, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe have adapted Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman's "keep dancing" move for threeByIan YoungsCulture reporterStrictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.Image caption, The new hosts joined the judges on the dance floor when the series beganAfter they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding".Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external.And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem."He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News."I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."Image caption, Widdicombe has been at the centre of comic sketches with the other hosts and judgesThe problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous."They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in."Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him"."But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.Image caption, Emma Willis has hosted shows including Big Brother and The VoiceRadio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in."I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less."They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds."It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly."Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."Image caption, One episode featured Widdicombe and Willis in a Mary Poppins-inspired sketchFrost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests."Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".Image source, Guy Levy / Ray Burmiston / BBCImage caption, Radebe has already gained a reputation for his flamboyant fashionBut while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain."JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast."He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable."And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.Image caption, The presenting trio watched on as Dame Sarah Storey and dance partner Julian Caillon were eliminated last weekendDr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled"."I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says."He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well."Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell."And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

schema.headline: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?

title: Brazil election: How a changing working class is reshaping the presidential race
description: Image caption, A student at a rally for President Lula da SilvaByIone WellsReporting fromSão Paulo and Rio de JaneiroIn the sprawling former industria
body: Image caption, A student at a rally for President Lula da SilvaByIone WellsReporting fromSão Paulo and Rio de JaneiroIn the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed São Paulo's "Silicon Valley."The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.Like many of Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up."We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers. "Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics – even though Flávio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.Image caption, Tairine says high prices are a problem for her"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.Flávio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.A new working classFor his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments."There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.Image caption, Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support BolsonaroRichard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro – Flavio's father and Brazil's president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil. But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the UN's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" in which people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending."Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.Lula's comeback strategyIn some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people – particularly students – on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in São Paulo attracted about a million people."A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.Image caption, Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is electedIn Maré, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in Maré, Vitoria, earns less than £300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off, and providing essential medicines for free.She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.Another resident, Andreza Dionísio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."Image caption, Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em CristoIncreasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus Vitória em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. He is being investigated for allegedly obstructing the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro, which he denies and calls politically motivated.At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine"."It gives these people meaning. To better their lives."Image caption, Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's weddingHe argues Flávio Bolsonaro shares the church's values: for family, and against gender "ideology" and abortion.The church is driving some to actively vote for Flávio Bolsonaro, but among much of Brazil's new working class, the first round feels more like a rejection of President Lula than an endorsement of his rival."There will never be another Lula," Gilberto Almazan fears. He intends this as a compliment, but Brazil's changing world of work means it's also probably true.While Lula's past story still stirs great emotion for people like Almazan, his political fate may depend on whether voters think he can now offer Brazil a new one.

schema.headline: Brazil election: How a changing working class is reshaping the presidential race

title: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?
description: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.Behind him,
body: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one.Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden.The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday.But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character. Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments. Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return.And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community". The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture.But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns.Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls."Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase."Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities". When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant"."Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent."I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's."Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations. Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview."I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer."When discussing the forthcoming sequel on CBS on Tuesday, Baron Cohen's "primary objective" appeared less ideological - to "get people to laugh really hard". Though he added that "smuggled in there is a bit of satire".In a new essay in Time this week, external, Baron Cohen argued that his characters have always been "vehicles to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity", and that in the case of Ali G, "the joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment" he aims to expose."The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him," Baron Cohen wrote."The world he's returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven't just lingered - they've metastasized. They're fueled by the greatest propaganda machine in history - social media - and now by its monstrous child, AI."The actor is no stranger to putting himself in potentially dangerous situations for his comedy. In a previous film, he infiltrated a gun rally, disguised as a "right-wing singer", while secretly wearing a bulletproof vest. Once members of the crowd realised they were being mocked, Baron Cohen was escorted into a getaway vehicle as an angry crowd "started pounding on the vehicle with their fists".Judging by Baron Cohen's description of the upcoming film, there may be further potential for danger. He told CBS he wanted to examine "conspiracies and lies" and test whether "we, in a matter of hours, could turn intelligent people who believed in the theory of race replacement into murderers".Colton Dunn, one of the film's black writers, questioned why Baron Cohen would put himself in danger, where interview subjects might react violently, if his intentions were racist. "From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists," Dunn told Deadline."That's why I signed on. I wouldn't sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that's against everything that I've done," he added.Almost 25 years on, Ali G still has loyal fans - including in his "home town" of Staines, in Surrey.Staines-upon-Thames resident Alex Balkan, who campaigned for a statue of Ali G in the town, says the character remains a source of local pride.While acknowledging not everyone welcomes the proposal, he says Ali G put Staines on the map."Everyone knows about us because of Ali G, and many of us wear that as a badge of pride," he says.  "It's a great conversation starter. It feels nice that people know about your town."Asked about accusations of racial stereotyping, Balkan believes the character is designed to be seen as a white man attempting to put on a stereotypical gangster persona, rather than to poke fun at black culture itself.One of the character's defenders is one of his most famous prank victims, politician Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg. "It is clever, satirical humour which makes the country, and many of us look foolish, and that's no bad thing," Sir Jacob posted on his social media. While some argue that audiences may have moved on from Ali G, supporters of the character contend that objections to his return reflect growing concerns about creative freedom in comedy. Balkan goes further, arguing that people today are more easily offended than they were two decades ago."This excessive zeal of political correctness, of left-wing po-facery, is crazy," Sir Jacob said. "It's a joke, it's comedy and it is poking fun at society as it is, as the best comedy often does."It would be unwise to judge the film before audiences have seen it. But the controversy surrounding its release suggests that, more than two decades after Ali G first appeared, the debate over who exactly is being laughed at is far from settled.

schema.headline: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?

title: Canada 31-22 England: Red Roses suffer back-to-back losses to Canada
description: WXV Global SeriesCanada (12) 31Tries: Omokhuale, De Goede 3, Bauder Cons: De Goede 3England (7) 22Tries: Feaunati, Cokayne, Sing Cons: Harrison, Sing
body: WXV Global SeriesCanada (12) 31Tries: Omokhuale, De Goede 3, Bauder Cons: De Goede 3England (7) 22Tries: Feaunati, Cokayne, Sing Cons: Harrison, Sing Pens: HarrisonHead coach John Mitchell said England need a "new stimulus" after losing 31-22 to Canada in the WXV Series in Ottawa to suffer back-to-back defeats for the first time in a decade.The hosts ran in five tries to England's three, including a hat-trick for captain Sophie de Goede, as they backed up last weekend's 24-21 win in Toronto, which ended the Red Roses' 41-match unbeaten streak, with another statement victory.It completes a 2-0 series win for Canada after the two sides also shared a 26-26 draw in Exeter in September. After losing multiple matches in a calendar year for the first time since 2016, world champions England head into their meeting with the USA in New Jersey next Friday (21:15 GMT) hoping to avoid three consecutive losses for the first time since 2013.England made a promising start, Maddie Feaunati crashing over from close range inside 10 minutes, but Canada hit back twice in quick succession through Julia Omokhuale and De Goede to lead 12-7 at the break.Zoe Harrison kicked a penalty early in the second half before England turned to their driving maul to overturn the deficit, Amy Cokayne walking in their second score.However, De Goede restored her side's lead three minutes later and completed her hat-trick just after the hour-mark before Savannah Bauder danced down the left wing to put Canada out of sight.Emma Sing bagged a consolation try for England in the 80th minute."Perhaps we have become a little bit predictable," said Mitchell, who arrived in Canada unbeaten as England head coach. "Definitely I'll have to create with the girls the new stimulus in the new year."Test matches of this quality, the best teams in the world, it always comes down to execution. We presented ourselves many an opportunity and we just didn't quite execute."This series has been a landmark occasion for women's rugby, with a record crowd for a standalone women's fixture in North America in attendance in Toronto last weekend for Canada's first home match since August 2025.The Maple Leafs had not beaten England since 2016 and had never done so on home soil. Now, they have done it twice in a row.But for all the positives, both for Canada and the growth of women's rugby, Mitchell called for "improved standards" around officiating, with connection issues to the television match official (TMO) influencing a "turning point" in the match.Heading into the final 20 minutes, with the match evenly poised 19-17 in Canada's favour, England winger Jess Breach's eyes lit up as she intercepted a pass from Justine Pelletier.The park opened up in front of her for a try which would have moved her into joint-second in the all-time list for England women, but she was pulled back mid-stride for being offside. Moments later, De Goede scored Canada's fourth to put them seven points ahead."The game potentially needs an improved standard with TMO," said Mitchell. "There was no TMO connection tonight and I think Jess' intercept was probably a turning point that could have influenced the match."There has been a TMO in the two Test matches but there has been no connection in the stadium. We've definitely got to improve on that. These games are so meaningful and there's going to be situation where they can be major turning points. The girls deserve quality decision-making."In the aftermath of Canada's World Cup final defeat by England last September, De Goede received her women's player of the year gong. Hoisted onto her team-mates' shoulders, she held the trophy aloft, albeit probably not the one she wanted to have her hands on in the moment.She saw off competition from England's Meg Jones and New Zealand's Jorja Miller to become only the second Canadian - man or woman - to win the accolade in 15s.Against England over the past six weeks, she has demonstrated why she is among the best in the world.It was her break down the left wing in Exeter which set up Olivia Apps' game-levelling try.In Ottawa, her versatility was on full display. She charged down the left wing as Senft's support runner for her first try, capitalised on a lapse in concentration from the other 29 players on the park to pick up a loose ball for her second - even having time to raise her arm in celebration, and dotted over for a classic second-row score from a maul to round out her performance.Kicking from her signature red tee - another example of the rising profile of the sport in Canada - she made eight of her 13 conversion attempts across the series. The two she missed in Ottawa were from the left touchline.Canada: Bauder; Corrigan, Symonds, Seumanutafa, Hogan-Rochester; Perry, Apps; Nelson, Idowu, Menin, De Goede (c), Royer, Senft, Omokhuale, Gibson. Replacements: Tuttosi, Kassil, Rempel, Forteza, Buisa, Crossley, Pelletier, Tessier.England: Sing; Breach, Jones (c), Rowland, Venner; Harrison, L Packer; Botterman, Cokayne, Bern, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Kabeya, Feaunati.Replacements: Field, Carson, Muir, Short, Matthews, Robinson, Aitchison, Kildunne.
