title: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad
description: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadImage caption, Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseasByElizabeth
body: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadImage caption, Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseasByElizabeth AndersonBusiness reporterLast year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place."I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey, external of 15,000 final year university students.Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high. UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report, external.For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?Australia: 'The weather's beautiful, even in the winter'While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show., externalIn addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme,, external British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.Image source, Rachel JamesImage caption, Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than LondonRachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched."People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."The US: 'I'm paid a lot more here'Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures, external from the UK's Office for National Statistics.It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.Image source, Charlie WestImage caption, Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunitiesCharlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching."I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live."In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."Europe: 'If you can work across the EU there are more opportunities'The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.Image source, Owein IvesonImage caption, Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from FinlandThis is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020."Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon."To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas. "When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London. "I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Let us know

title: US Grand Prix: Charles Leclerc sets Austin practice pace from Kimi Antonelli
description: Ferrari's Charles Leclerc led Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in Friday practice at the United States Grand Prix - but Max Verstappen left the strongest impr
body: Ferrari's Charles Leclerc led Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in Friday practice at the United States Grand Prix - but Max Verstappen left the strongest impression in his Red Bull.Leclerc, who topped both sessions, was 0.042 seconds ahead of the Italian, who has a mathematical chance of tying up his first world title this weekend.Antonelli will win the championship in Austin only if he wins the race and team-mate George Russell finishes below eighth and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton below fourth.Verstappen was third fastest, 0.189secs back, ahead of Hamilton, although the seven-time champion was 0.615secs off the pace. Russell was fifth ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson.Verstappen appeared fastest on the race-simulation runs later in the session, which often provide a more accurate read of overall competitiveness than the single laps.The Dutchman could be compared directly only with the Ferrari drivers, as all were running the soft-compound tyres on their long runs.Verstappen was marginally faster than Leclerc on average but the consistency of his pace suggested he was in the best shape, at least on Friday.Hamilton appeared to be struggling for pace compared with Leclerc whether on short runs or long.Ferrari have an upgrade on their car this weekend, focused on a new floor, but Leclerc was downplaying expectations."It felt good but it is not the gain I have seen or heard about," Leclerc said. "It is small gains but we could still see them on the car. It is a small step forward and we started the weekend on the right foot with a good balance and that is the outstanding thing with this Friday."It has been a very clean Friday for me, but the others seem to be gaining more than us from Friday to Saturday and seeing the little gap there is, it is not going to be so easy tomorrow."Leclerc picked up on Verstappen's complaints about the track surface on Thursday by saying: "It was very poor. The first sector is particularly poor and very bumpy."McLaren's Lando Norris was seventh fastest, although the world champion did not set a time on his qualifying simulation run on soft tyres after making a mistake at Turn 16.Norris was the fastest on the long runs, at about 0.2secs on average faster than Verstappen, but cannot be compared as he was running the hard tyre.McLaren have introduced the first of three consecutive planned upgrades this weekend, but he was not happy with his performance."Difficult," Norris said. "The pace is not bad. We seem a step away from Red Bull and Ferrari, probably Mercedes as well, but the car is very difficult to drive, too difficult to be consistent and get a nice feeling consistently."To get the car be quick we just have to try so hard to be perfect and you can't be perfect. I am sure everyone has similar problems in a way but we are just not quick enough yet to be there consistently enough."McLaren's Oscar Piastri was eighth quickest, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar and Haas driver Oliver Bearman.

schema.headline: US Grand Prix: Charles Leclerc sets Austin practice pace from Kimi Antonelli
